problems.description: Flattened the seed's modular Blueprint-based structure into a single app.py that mixes routing, DB access, and request handling inline. The seed explicitly documents 'A modular Flask app with Blueprints' as the baseline for multi-session tier-2 stories, so later sessions must refactor this back out to grow the app.

8 naming-convention violations (classes should be PascalCase, module constants UPPER_CASE, functions snake_case) across app.py, celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py — convention score 0.73.

Removed the seed's auth/roles layer (users, tokens, require_auth decorator) entirely; if the task manager story later needs multi-user or protected endpoints, that infrastructure must be reintroduced rather than extended.

strengths: Directionally correct for the story: replaces the generic auth seed with the task-manager domain (POST/GET /tasks backed by SQLite persistence).
SonarQube delta is strictly positive — cognitive complexity -10, smells -2, 0 new bugs, 0 duplications.
Preserves the seed's get_db/init_db pattern and env-var DATABASE configuration, and adds a repositories.py data layer plus Celery scaffolding consistent with the story ecosystem.
Includes tests (test_app.py) with input validation and proper HTTP status codes (400/201).
commit_reviews.summary: Greenfield session correctly redirects the auth-API seed toward a task-manager API with measurably simpler code (complexity -10, smells -2), but flattens the seed's modular Blueprint architecture into a single app.py and lands 8 minor naming-convention violations (score 0.73).

problems.description: Hardcoded fallback SECRET_KEY ('dev-secret-change-me-in-production!') signs all JWTs when the env var is absent — any deployment that forgets to set it ships forgeable tokens. A fallback should at least fail or warn loudly.

The migration's 'legacy' owner gets a password hash baked into source ('legacy-default-password') — anyone who reads the repo can log in as legacy and read every pre-existing task, defeating the data-preservation intent.
Login has no brute-force protection and tokens cannot be revoked/blacklisted; acceptable for this scope but worth noting.
int(user_id) in get_user_from_token is unguarded against a malformed 'sub' claim (jwt.decode catches type errors, but the conversion itself can raise).
Migration uses PRAGMA column-sniffing rather than a versioned schema; pragmatic at this scale but does not scale to later migrations.

strengths: Idempotent, data-preserving migration: owner_id added via ALTER TABLE and orphans reassigned to a legacy owner, so existing data is not dropped.
Ownership is scoped into every query (WHERE owner_id = ?) on all task endpoints, preventing cross-user data access.
Uses @functools.wraps on the auth decorator and werkzeug salted password hashing + PyJWT with an expiry claim — correct auth primitives.
Follows existing patterns: same get_db context-manager usage, task_to_dict response shape, and response conventions across all modified endpoints.
Consistent with the existing datetime.utcnow() convention and UPPER_CASE module constants (SECRET_KEY, JWT_ALGORITHM, TOKEN_TTL).
commit_reviews.summary: A coherent, data-preserving feature addition (auth + task ownership) that respects the existing single-file Flask/SQLite patterns, but the hardcoded fallback secret and legacy account password introduce real security debt, and the 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py) rather than this diff's own code.

problems.description: When a user has no email, the notification falls back to `user_email = user.get("email") or user["username"]`, so a 'notification email' is dispatched to a username — semantically wrong; better to skip the notification or send only when an email exists.
celery_app.py duplicates output with both `logger.info(message)` and `print(message)` in the task; pick one logging channel.
Notification trigger logic lives inline in the update_task request handler rather than as a domain/event seam; acceptable at this app's scale but couples the HTTP layer to the async side-effect.
Tests patch `delay` but never exercise `CELERY_TASK_ALWAYS_EAGER`; the eager-path task body is untested.
Task is routed to an "email" queue, but no worker/queue-consumption setup is documented; undispatched tasks would silently accumulate if no worker runs.

The mechanical score (0.73, 8 violations) appears inflated by heuristic false positives — e.g. 'snake_case functions' in celery_config.py which contains none, and 'PascalCase classes' in app.py/test_app.py. Qualitative review finds the actual code follows conventions (CeleryConfig PascalCase, namespaced task name, snake_case funcs).

strengths: Clean separation of concerns: Celery app (celery_app.py) split from config (celery_config.py) with env-overridable broker/backend and eager mode.
Migration extended idempotently, following the existing migrate() pattern exactly (PRAGMA check → ALTER → commit).
Notification fires only on a status *transition* to completed, correctly skipping re-completion of already-completed tasks.
Thorough test coverage: trigger, non-trigger, re-completion dedupe, and 404 paths all tested with delay mocked.
Defensive enqueue wrapped in try/except with app.logger.exception; no import cycle (celery_app imports config only, not app).
commit_reviews.summary: Well-structured async notification feature that cleanly respects the app's existing migration/config/test patterns and adds solid transition-trigger tests; the low convention score (0.73) is largely driven by heuristic false positives, with only minor real nitpicks (email→username fallback, print/logger duplication).

problems.description: BaseRepository builds SQL by f-string-interpolating column names in create()/update()/delete()/get_by_id(). Values are parameterized and current callers pass trusted literal keys, so it is not exploitable today, but the generic **values API makes identifier injection trivial if any caller ever derives keys from request data — a fragile footgun for a shared base class.

Every repository call opens a fresh sqlite3 connection; create() and update() open a second one for the post-write get_by_id() re-query, dropping the single-connection-per-operation idiom and doubling round-trips on the write path.

_connect() re-implements the app's existing get_db() factory (sqlite3.connect + row_factory) instead of composing with it, splitting connection logic across two files and letting the idioms drift (e.g., PRAGMA foreign_keys is set in get_db() but not in repositories).

The new repositories.py introduces a lowercase module-level constant (SonarQube 'Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE'); the other measured violations live in files this commit did not touch (celery_app.py, celery_config.py, test_app.py) and the app.py PascalCase flag is pre-existing.
No tests accompany the new repository layer; behavior is preserved for existing test_app.py but the repo methods (find_by_username, list_by_owner, update) are untested in isolation.

strengths: Clean separation of persistence from route handlers — DB access is confined to repositories.py and handlers become declarative.
All values are parameterized; only table/column identifiers are interpolated, from a small trusted set.
An abstract BaseRepository with shared CRUD removes per-table duplication and gives the layer a single seam for future schema work.
The refactor is localized and behavior-preserving across the touched endpoints (auth, task CRUD), removing the task_to_dict helper.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive repository-pattern refactor that keeps handlers free of raw SQL and is largely convention-clean on its own diff, but the mechanical 0.73 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files, and the generic f-string CRUD plus per-call connection churn introduce modest new technical debt.

problems.description: Fixture reaches into flask-limiter private internals (limiter._storage, _limiter, _storage_dead, _strategy) to swap in fakeredis — fragile across library upgrades and version-pins the test to an undocumented implementation.
_rate_limit_key re-implements JWT decode inline in app.py instead of reusing the auth path already owned by require_auth, duplicating token-handling logic and its exception surface in a second place.
_rate_limit_value is a trivial passthrough wrapper; the indirection adds no real value over referencing RATE_LIMIT directly, and its runtime-read of the module global is easy to misread.
paginate_by_owner issues a full COUNT(*) on every page; acceptable at this scale but wasteful across many pages.
One global '100 per minute' limit applies uniformly to all routes including auth endpoints, so per-IP login brute-force protection is weak (100 attempts/min); per-route limits would be tighter.

strengths: Pagination correctly placed in the repository layer (paginate_by_owner) matching TaskRepository's existing method/query patterns — good architectural layering.
Keyset/cursor pagination with a limit+1 has-more probe avoids OFFSET scanning and cleanly signals end-of-stream via null next_cursor.
Robust input handling: limit clamped to 1..100, invalid cursor returns 400, response shape ({data, next_cursor, total}) is consistent and versioned as a single change.
Rate limiting keyed by authenticated user id with IP fallback, headers_enabled, and env-configurable storage/limits — a standard, well-scoped flask-limiter setup.
Tests cover both the paginated shape and full cursor walk, plus existing tests updated to the new response envelope.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid commit — cursor pagination and user-aware rate limiting implemented at the right layers with good tests and input validation, but the fixture's reach into flask-limiter private attributes and the duplicated JWT decode are minor debts; the measured 0.73 convention score is driven by pre-existing whole-file violations (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants) that this diff did not introduce — the diff's own additions are snake_case/UPPER_CASE compliant, so my qualitative read is higher than the raw score.

compounding_issues: No requirements.txt or dependency manifest was ever added, despite the agent introducing PyJWT (s2), Celery (s3), and flask-limiter/fakeredis/redis (s5) — the project is not reproducible in a fresh environment and later sessions depended on the runner's pre-installed site-packages.

Session 3's module-level `from celery_app import send_notification_email` makes app.py unimportable if Celery is absent, and with the broker defaulting to redis://localhost:6379/0 (eager off), completion emails silently no-op wherever no broker runs (the try/except swallows the failure).

Session 5's rate limiter storage also defaults to redis://localhost:6379/0 with no fallback; tests only pass by injecting a fakeredis pool into the limiter internals, so out-of-the-box runtime behavior is coupled to an external Redis that is not declared anywhere.
Session 1's greenfield rewrite discarded the seed's auth scaffolding wholesale, so JWT authentication and per-owner scoping had to be rebuilt from scratch in session 2 rather than evolved.
key_decisions: Session 1: full clean-slate rewrite — minimal single-file task CRUD on SQLite with init_db() at import time, replacing the seed auth API.

Session 2: JWT auth via PyJWT + owner_id data scoping + idempotent ALTER TABLE migrations that preserve pre-existing rows by assigning them to a 'legacy' user — the decision that let the schema grow across sessions without data loss.
Session 3: Celery async task boundary (mock email notification) plus a users.email column added through the same inline migration mechanism.
Session 4: repository layer extraction (BaseRepository ABC with TaskRepository/UserRepository), removing raw SQL from route handlers and setting up the seam session 5 exploits.
Session 5: flask-limiter app-wide rate limiting keyed per authenticated user id, plus keyset cursor pagination (ORDER BY id DESC, id < cursor) implemented on the session-4 repository.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions. The test suite grew monotonically from 8 to 16 to 20 to 20 to 32 tests, with a fully green run at every commit. The architecture progressed from a flat single-module scaffold to a layered design — routes in app.py, query logic in a repository layer, and an async worker in celery_app.py — with cross-cutting concerns (auth, ownership, notifications, rate limiting, pagination) added in a sensible order that built on prior sessions, most notably session 5's pagination sitting cleanly on the session-4 repository abstraction. The persistent weakness was engineering hygiene around dependencies: new libraries were adopted session after session without ever being declared, so the code quality rose while the project's reproducibility never did.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, textbook five-session progression from minimal CRUD scaffold through auth, async integration, a repository-layer refactor, and cross-cutting hardening, with a steadily growing and always-green test suite — marred only by never formalizing dependency management.
